title: Rapid screening of target-specific isotope labeling protocols for in situ NMR of bacterial membrane proteins
abstract: We describe an approach for the efficient development of targeted isotope labeling protocols leading to nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) structural studies of bacterial membrane proteins in intact cells and native outer membrane (OM) vesicles (OMVs). The assay relies on the bioorthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging (BONCAT) approach for metabolic incorporation of an azide-bearing residue, followed by copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) to an alkyne-functionalized fluorescent dye. Fluorescence detection in SDS-PAGE provides a rapid way to test samples for off-target background signal from endogenous proteins, bypassing the need for intensive NMR screening experiments. Using this approach, we develop an optimized protocol that enables high-resolution NMR spectra to be obtained in situ with negligible background signal. The BONCAT approach also enables target-specific fluorescence or nano-gold labeling of proteins at the OM surface, further extending the utility of this protocol for correlative structure-activity studies of membrane proteins in situ.

title: Traumatic microbleeds are associated with unfavorable outcome out to 1 year after mild traumatic brain injury
abstract: Importance: Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are commonly observed in mild TBI (mTBI). However, questions remain regarding their long-term prognostic significance. Objective: Determine whether traumatic microbleeds predict unfavorable outcome after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) Design: The prospective longitudinal observational Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury (TRACK-TBI) study enrolled acute TBI patients presenting to Emergency Departments (ED) at 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers between 2/26/2014-08/08/2018. CT and MRI were evaluated using the National Institutes of Health National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH NINDS) TBI Common Data Elements. Outcome was assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale Extended (GOSE-TBI) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury. Setting: 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers Participants: 929 GCS 13-15 patients at least 17 years of age (38.5 +/- 16.5 years, 66% male) who underwent clinical head CT <24 hours after injury and brain MRI at 2 weeks post-injury and had at least one GOSE-TBI outcome score during 1 year follow-up. Exposure(s): Acute non-penetrating head trauma Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s): Frequency and co-occurrence of CT and MR features; incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. 8) and unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5 vs. >=5) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months Results: Generalized estimating equation models showed that TMBs and/or IVH were strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5 vs. >=5) at 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury, but not with incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8). For prediction of GOSE-TBI <5 vs. >=5 TMBs surpassed the importance of all demographic and baseline clinical predictors throughout the 1-year follow-up period. For prediction of incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8), brain contusions, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and subdural hematoma were more important throughout the 12-month follow-up period. Conclusions and Relevance: Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are common in mTBI. The presence of 4 or more TMBs and/or IVH is strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5) after mTBI out to at least 1 year, even after controlling for other neuroimaging abnormalities and demographic and clinical predictors. Better understanding of the implications of TMBs for long-term functional outcome may inform rehabilitation planning.

title: Manifestation-Guided Adaptation of CT Foundation Model for Early Neurological Prognosis after ECPR
abstract: Purpose. To develop a data-efficient, clinically guided transfer-learning framework for hyperacute neurological outcome prediction from head CT in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) after cardiac arrest by leveraging free-text radiology report. Methods. This retrospective study included 683 patients with available CT examination and radiology reports from December 2015 to November 2025. The primary outcome distinguished favorable neurological outcomes (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2) from neurological death due to brain death or cerebral herniation (CPC 5). A cross-attention adaptor jointly learned to predict neurological outcome and five report-derived manifestations of brain injury from a frozen pretrained head CT encoder. Outcome prediction used CT images alone at inference. The manifestation-guided adaptor, trained with and without additional patients who contributed only manifestation labels, was compared with outcome-only adaptor and two pooled-feature baselines. Performance was summarized as mean {+/-} SD across five held-out folds. Results. Of 683 patients, 197 were eligible for outcome evaluation (63 with favorable outcomes and 134 with neurological death), and 486 formed the manifestation-only cohort. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.918 {+/-} 0.044 for the outcome-only adaptor. The manifestation-guided adaptor achieved an AUROC of 0.927 {+/-} 0.042. With additional manifestation-only training data, the adaptor achieved the mean AUROC (0.929 {+/-} 0.037), specificity (93.7% {+/-} 6.5%), with a sensitivity of 79.9% {+/-} 9.2%. Conclusion. Manifestation-guided adaptation outperforms outcome-only adaptation for neurological outcome prediction from hyperacute head CT after ECPR. Report-derived manifestation labels enabled training with additional examinations without eligible outcome labels while preserving CT-only prediction.

title: Age and sex differences in lateral ventricle choroid plexus volume in a large, manually segmented, multi-site MRI dataset
abstract: Background The choroid plexus, which produces cerebrospinal fluid and forms the blood–cerebrospinal fluid barrier, is of growing interest in psychiatric and neurodegenerative neuroimaging. However, most volumetric studies have relied on automated segmentation tools that agree poorly with manual tracing, and manually segmented samples have been small, single-site, and narrow in age range. Methods We analyzed DataPlex, a dataset of 700 manually segmented lateral ventricle choroid plexus labels from 3T T1-weighted MRI scans (ages 6–90 years) drawn from 29 studies and three scanner manufacturers (35 study-by-manufacturer sites). Generalized least squares models accounting for within-site dependence tested associations of age, sex, scanner manufacturer, image resolution, a registration-based image-quality metric, and intracranial volume with choroid plexus and lateral ventricle volumes, including nonlinear (spline) and sex-interaction terms. Exploratory models tested associations between these volumes and cognitive performance. Results In 699 scans, choroid plexus volume increased linearly with age (63–69 mm³ per decade) and was 56–65 mm³ larger in males than females after covariate adjustment; the age association did not differ by sex. Lateral ventricle volume increased nonlinearly with age, with steeper age-related enlargement in males than females. Scanner manufacturer and image resolution were associated with left lateral ventricle volume; scanner manufacturer was associated with choroid plexus volume only in a sensitivity model. The image-quality metric was not associated with any outcome. In exploratory analyses, larger choroid plexus volume was associated with lower inhibitory control, working memory, and episodic memory scores and with higher emotion recognition scores (uncorrected p < 0.05). Conclusions In the largest and most diverse manually segmented choroid plexus dataset to date, choroid plexus volume differed by age and sex and was less sensitive than lateral ventricle volume to acquisition differences. These estimates provide reference benchmarks for automated segmentation tools and support adjustment for demographic and technical covariates.

title: Patient, carer and clinical stakeholder views on using artificial intelligence and machine learning for the histopathological diagnosis of duodenal biopsies
abstract: Objective Biopsies are examined under the microscope by a pathologist, giving a diagnosis, which guides treatment and predicts prognosis. A shortage of pathologists and increasing workload leads to diagnostic delays, while for duodenal (small intestinal) biopsies, variable diagnostic concordance between pathologists limits accuracy. These challenges have motivated us to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated approach for the automated diagnosis of up to 80% of duodenal biopsies (i.e., most cases of the two most frequent diagnoses: coeliac disease and “normal”). We set out to understand patient, carer and stakeholder views regarding the adoption of such technology. Methods and Analysis We conducted mixed-methods stakeholder engagement (February 2024 to June 2026). We ran a national online patients’ and carers’ questionnaire (n=231 respondents) and four UK focus-group workshops, one of which additionally captured Likert-scale attitudes 1 immediately before and after a structured educational session (n=34 matched pairs). Healthcare professionals completed an online questionnaire (n=37) and took part in a structured workshop. Quantitative data were summarised descriptively; free-text and workshop data were analysed thematically and triangulated across all sources. Results Most patients and carers supported AI-reliant diagnosis (68.4%) and would strongly trust systems with formal regulatory approval (66.7%). Most wanted to be informed if AI was used (73.6%), but only 52.4% felt explicit permission was necessary. Qualitative themes centred on clear and available evidence of accuracy, human oversight, transparent communication and clear terminology, with the term ‘machine learning’ being preferred to ‘artificial intelligence’. Agreement (‘agree’ or ‘strongly agree’ combined) with statements relating to trust, acceptance and perceived benefit of AI was significantly higher after a structured educational session (38.2% to 67.6%, 85.3% to 97.1%, and 52.9% to 97.1% respectively; all p≤0.003). Healthcare professionals favoured an AI ‘assistant’ model over full automation, citing the need for validation, explainability, data governance and workflow integration. Patients also preferred some level of human oversight. Conclusion Patients and healthcare professionals are cautiously supportive of AI-assisted diagnosis of duodenal biopsies, conditional upon demonstration of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication. Attitudes towards AI-assisted diagnosis were more favourable after structured explanation. Key Messages What is already known on this topic Very little is known about patients’, carers’ or healthcare professionals’ views about the automation of diagnosis in pathology, using AI-based software solutions. What this study adds ⇒ This is the first study to investigate patient, carer and healthcare professional attitudes specifically to AI-mediated duodenal biopsy diagnosis. Around two-thirds of respondents supported AI-assisted diagnosis, contingent upon clear and available evidence of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication, together with appropriate regulatory approval of the technology. ⇒ Attitudes were markedly more favourable after a single structured educational session: agreement that AI could improve duodenal biopsy diagnosis nearly doubled and trust in healthcare AI rose substantially, suggesting that public views of AI in diagnosis can be influenced by clear explanation. ⇒ Patients and healthcare professionals both favour some ongoing level of human oversight of any AI-based diagnostic approach. How this study might affect research, practice or policy ⇒ Our study suggests that a phased, AI-assistant-first deployment model with defined validation and audit checkpoints would be most readily acceptable when introducing diagnostic AI into histopathology. ⇒ It indicates that appropriate information and education, for example, a patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) session, can increase trust in AI in healthcare. ⇒ It shows that patients and the public are more trusting of technology for which the term machine learning is used, rather than artificial intelligence (AI). ⇒ It offers a stakeholder-engagement template for use by others introducing AI-based diagnostics.

title: Automated segmentation of renal structures using brightfield images of unstained kidney biopsies
abstract: The automated segmentation of unstained kidney brightfield microscopy images remains a significant challenge in medical imaging. In conventional histopathology, staining provides crucial structural and molecular contrast, allowing renal compartments and structures to be readily distinguished. The absence of staining markedly reduces this contrast, obscuring the fine architectural details that are essential for diagnosis. Addressing this gap would reduce reliance on staining protocols, reduce technical and interpretive variability, and preserve valuable tissue for downstream molecular or multi-omics analyses. Ultimately, automation of unstained image segmentation could enable faster, more objective tissue analysis while preserving samples for further molecular testing. In this work, we provide a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art segmentation methods applied to renal brightfield microscopy images. Current findings highlight a predominance of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based architectures for semantic segmentation approaches while recent trends point to the growing application of transformer-based and instance-segmentation strategies. However, the field is still hampered by the scarcity and poor annotation of publicly available renal datasets. Aiming to further contribute to the enhancement of the field, a dataset of 18 Whole Slide Images (WSIs) of unstained human kidney tissue is made publicly available. Additionally, in the dataset, we provide 543 annotated tiles extracted from the WSIs, facilitating further research into stain-independent segmentation approaches. As a third contribution, we present a preliminary case study, evaluating state-of-the-art deep learning segmentation architectures, including U-Net and Segment Anything Model (SAM). Our preliminary results indicate that deep learning models demonstrate promising segmentation performance in unstained kidney biopsies. In alignment with these findings, advanced customised loss functions and data augmentation were integrated into the supervised training of the promising U-Net, DeepLabv3+, and TransUNet models, achieving significant improvements compared to the baseline experiments. To exploit the abundance of unlabelled data, we further tested FixMatchSeg, a semi-supervised learning method; however, its segmentation performance remained slightly behind the supervised methods. Taken together, these contributions establish a foundation for future research in stain-independent Computational Pathology, demonstrating that unstained brightfield microscopy images can reliably support downstream tissue analysis tasks. Our dataset, validation experiments, and methodological insights provide the community with both resources and benchmarks to advance robust, data-efficient, and generalisable kidney tissue segmentation.

title: Automated Gland MRI Radiomics for Predicting Time to Pathologic Progression during Prostate Cancer Active Surveillance
abstract: Background: Repeated biopsies burden patients during prostate cancer active surveillance (AS). Existing MRI risk stratification tools avoiding biopsy remain limited by the difficulty of automated lesion segmentation. Purpose: To develop a model integrating gland MRI radiomics and clinicopathologic variables for predicting time to pathologic progression during prostate cancer AS. Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-institution study included men with grade group 1 or favorable grade group 2 prostate cancer undergoing AS with fusion-targeted and systematic biopsy (2010-2025). Gland segmentation used nnU-Net; gland radiomic features were selected by LASSO-penalized survival regression to train an XGBoost accelerated failure time model. Comparator models were assessed by C-index, time-dependent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), Kaplan-Meier, and decision curve analysis. Results: Of 522 men (median age, 64 years [IQR, 59-68]), 410 were assigned by site to development and 112 to internal testing. Gland segmentation Dice was 0.89 +/- 0.04. The C-index was higher for the gland radiomics model (0.77) than for clinicopathologic (0.68) and lesion radiomics (0.68) models (adjusted P [≤] .017), with the highest time-dependent AUC at 36 months (0.87 [95% CI: 0.78, 0.94]). Progression-free survival was lower in high-risk than low-risk groups (36 months, 63.9% vs 100%; 48 months, 55.4% vs 93.8%; log-rank P < .001). At a 0.25 risk threshold, 49.1% and 31.3% were low risk at 36 and 48 months (negative predictive value, 1.00; positive predictive value, 0.36). Conclusion: An automated gland radiomics model predicted time to pathologic progression during AS better than clinicopathologic and lesion-based models.

title: Virtual spatial transcriptomics links kidney histopathology to disease-associated molecular programs
abstract: Introduction: Spatial transcriptomics can resolve compartment-specific molecular programs in kidney disease, but its cost and technical requirements limit its use in clinical diagnostics and in large biopsy archives. Predicting spatial gene expression from routine histology with artificial intelligence could extend molecular characterization to existing clinically annotated kidney tissue collections. Methods: We adapted DeepSpot-M, a pretrained multimodal foundation model that predicts spatial gene expression from histology, using paired hematoxylin and eosin images and Visium spatial transcriptomics from 209 Kidney Precision Medicine Project (KPMP) participants. We evaluated virtual profiles in held-out human biopsies, associated them with histopathologic and biochemical injury markers in 567 rats with defined nephrotoxin exposures from a public toxicogenomics database, and generated a virtual atlas from 1,534 histology slides of 476 additional KPMP participants. Results: Kidney-specific adaptation of DeepSpot-M doubled the mean Pearson correlation of each model's 1,000 best-predicted genes (0.43 versus 0.22) and exceeded recent foundation models. Virtual profiles preserved the direction of all 13 disease-marker differences in measured expression, including tubular injury, maladaptive repair, gluconeogenesis, and fibrosis-associated programs. All 11 measured associations between molecular programs and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were also preserved. Without rat-specific training, a virtual injury score distinguished moderate or severe histopathologic lesions (area under the curve, 0.85) and at least twofold blood urea nitrogen elevation (0.82). In our atlas of 5.46 million virtual spots, higher proximal tubule program scores were associated with higher eGFR (partial r, 0.32) and less interstitial fibrosis (-0.57), and program-pathology associations agreed with those of measured Visium profiles in independent participants (Spearman rho, 0.64). Conclusions: Kidney-adapted virtual spatial transcriptomics links histology-derived molecular programs to experimental renal injury and human clinical and histologic phenotypes. Our approach enables spatial molecular analyses in routine biopsy histology, which could help decipher disease-associated pathways in existing biopsy archives.

title: Generative Deep Learning Maps Brain Oxygen Metabolism and Its Age-Related Decline from Two Standard Noninvasive MRI Scans
abstract: Purpose: To develop a generative deep learning model mapping the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2) from minimal, contrast-free MRI. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study used 3-T MRI of healthy adults from one center (May 2015-June 2025). A conditional generative adversarial network (GAN) was trained to reproduce contrast-based analytical CMRO2 from progressively fewer quantitative MRI inputs (cerebral blood flow [CBF], T2*, T2, cerebral blood volume), T1-weighted MRI, or resting-state functional MRI. Models were trained on 54 participants and tested on 41 (25 women; mean age, 49 years +/- 23 [SD]), on calculation-task data, and, without retraining, on same-protocol (n = 24) and cross-vendor (n = 12) data. Agreement (r, mean absolute error [MAE]) was compared with the test-retest error of analytical CMRO2, and repeatability (n = 9) with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Results: A GAN using only CBF and T2* agreed with analytical CMRO2 as well as one adding T2 (r = 0.89 [95% CI: 0.88, 0.90] for both), with errors below the between-day test-retest error (median MAE, 38.1 vs 46.5 micromol/100 g/min); CBF alone, T1-weighted MRI, and functional MRI performed worse (P <= .004). It was as repeatable as analytical CMRO2 (median ICC, 0.87 for both), preserved task-evoked patterns (Dice, 0.78), agreed with same-protocol (r = 0.89) and, less, cross-vendor data (r = 0.81; P <= .001), and captured the age-related decline (6.8 vs analytical, 5.0 micromol/100 g/min per decade). Conclusion: Generative deep learning mapped brain oxygen metabolism from two contrast-free scans with repeatability comparable to the reference.

title: Distinct Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging-Derived White Matter Microstructural Phenotypes Tracking Alzheimer's Disease Pathology and Cognitive Decline
abstract: White matter (WM) pathology is increasingly recognized as an early, mechanistically relevant feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet sensitive in-vivo biomarkers remain limited. Here, we introduce an MRI-based Relaxation Kurtosis Imaging (RKI) technique sensitive to WM microstructure. RKI metrics differentiate two distinct phenotypes of white matter that follow divergent microstructural trajectories in preclinical and early symptomatic AD. We examined their relationships to AD progression, gray matter (GM) pathology, and clinical impairment in 305 adults spanning amyloid-negative to amyloid-positive stages with normal cognition, preclinical AD, and early symptomatic AD. Pathological changes in one phenotype reflected axonal alterations without myelin loss and were anatomically coupled to GM cortical pathology, strengthening with disease stage - a signature of Wallerian degeneration. Alterations in the other phenotype represented WM demyelination. A model incorporating RKI-metrics, age, sex, amyloid status, APOE genotype, and brain volume classified Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR)-based impairment with an area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) = 0.933, with the RKI-metrics contributing 27% (second only to amyloid at 40%). While both phenotypes related comparably to concurrent cognition (each ~27%), the "axonal" phenotype showed the strongest relationship to subsequent cognitive decline (41% of explained variance), with the "myelin" phenotype contributing 31%. These RKI-defined dual white matter phenotypes provide new insight into AD pathology, adding diagnostic and prognostic value for tracking both current cognitive status and future cognitive decline.

title: Lightweight and Explainable AI for Chest Radiograph Classification in Low-Resource Settings: Cross-Dataset Generalization, Grad-CAM Verification, and Uncertainty-Aware Referral
abstract: Chest radiography is the most common imaging test worldwide, yet models trained on one hospital's data often fail elsewhere, a critical problem for low-resource hospitals that cannot collect large local datasets. This paper presents a lightweight, explainable framework for chest radiograph classification, trained and evaluated entirely on CPU with public data. EfficientNet-B0 and ResNet-18 are trained on a 10,000-image subset of NIH ChestX-ray14 and evaluated without retraining on a paediatric pneumonia set, alongside a TorchXRayVision DenseNet121 pretrained baseline and a model trained directly on paediatric data. On the NIH test set (n = 2,500), the best single model reaches pneumonia AUC-ROC 0.738 and a two-model ensemble 0.742, while an adult-trained model falls to AUC 0.454 on paediatric images, and, symmetrically, a paediatric-trained model falls to 0.473 on adult NIH images. Pooling the adult and paediatric training sets into one binary pneumonia model changes the picture: a merged EfficientNet-B0 reaches AUC 0.951 (95% CI 0.932-0.967) on paediatric images, the first result whose whole 95% CI clears 0.90, and 0.675 on NIH images with zero sensitivity at threshold 0.5, while a merged ResNet-18 reaches 0.962 on paediatric and 0.606 on NIH images. Pooling fixes the catastrophic cross-domain failure but does not recover adult-only performance, and ensembling a merged model with a single-domain model adds nothing on either test set. Grad-CAM heatmaps are shown for true positives, false negatives and false positives, and Monte Carlo dropout referral raises answered-case accuracy from 0.889 to 0.948 on NIH data but not under domain shift. All results carry bootstrap confidence intervals, and the limits of a 22-positive NIH test set are stated plainly.

title: Focused ultrasound-enhanced carboplatin delivery improves radiotherapy response and survival in a preclinical glioblastoma model
abstract: Rationale Glioblastoma is highly resistant to conventional therapies due to the limited penetration of chemotherapeutics across the blood-brain and blood-tumor barriers (BBB, BTB). Although platinum-based drugs show strong cytotoxic and radiosensitizing properties in several cancers, their inability to achieve therapeutic concentrations within the central nervous system (CNS) severely limits their efficacy in brain tumors. This study investigated whether focused ultrasound (FUS)-mediated BBB/BTB disruption combined with intravenous carboplatin and stereotactic radiotherapy could improve drug delivery, tumor control, and survival in a preclinical glioblastoma model. Methods F98 glioma-bearing rats were treated with a single dose of 15 Gy radiation therapy (RT), carboplatin only, carboplatin + RT, FUS + carboplatin or FUS + carboplatin + RT. FUS-mediated permeabilization was confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and platinum accumulation was quantified by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry and synchrotron X-ray fluorescence. Tumor progression and microenvironmental changes were monitored using multiparametric MRI (diffusion, perfusion, and vascular permeability), followed by voxel-wise clustering analysis and histopathological validation. Results The FUS + carboplatin + RT group demonstrated the strongest therapeutic benefit, compared to all other treatment groups, yielding up to a 122% increase in median survival relative to the untreated group. This treatment also reduced necrotic core expansion and induced a transient increase in tumor perfusion, suggesting improved vascular function. FUS enhanced carboplatin delivery to both the tumor and peritumoral brain, with platinum distribution closely correlating with MRI signal enhancement. Voxel-wise clustering of multiparametric MRI identified biologically distinct tumor regions that were subsequently validated by immunohistochemistry. Conclusion The combination of FUS-mediated carboplatin delivery and radiotherapy represents a safe, non-invasive strategy that enhances drug delivery and improves survival in an aggressive preclinical model of glioblastoma. By overcoming a major limitation of current therapies, this approach shows promising potential for clinical translation.

title: A Deep Operator Network to Predict Thermal Dose on Brain Tumors in MRI-Guided Laser Induced Thermal Therapy: with Synthetic Data
abstract: Background: MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) provides minimally invasive option for surgical treatment of recurrent brain tumors. While patient-specific prediction of thermal dose distributions would improve treatment planning, no quantitative methods currently exist for this purpose. Although conventional numerical solvers are being widely investigated, these methods are computationally expensive and often limited by accuracy and reliability. Purpose: Here we propose DeepoLITT, a rapid and accurate model to predict quantitatively heat propagation in LITT procedures. This study represents the first phase of the investigation which focuses on training and validating synthetic datasets to test model , s accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. Methods: We built DeepoLITT on a branch–trunk neural network architecture, where the first branch extracts feature from tumor images, the second branch encodes laser parameters (power, duration, and probe orientation), and the trunk models the mapping from spatial coordinates to the resulting temperature field. To train and test the model, we generated synthetic datasets with different noise levels (0~20%) to mimic LITT procedures with two distinct laser probe types (FullFire and SideFire [Monteris, Inc.]) by a FEM (finite element method) solver. The dataset consisted of 400 samples, of which 90% were used for training and validation and 10% for testing. To evaluate spatial similarity of predicted thermal dose distribution against the ground truth, we employed Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and Hausdorff Distance (HD) computed on CEM43 (Cumulative Equivalent Minutes at 43 °C) isodose contours at thresholds of 2, 10, and 60 minutes. Finally, we evaluated the model , s inference speed with a representative image grid. Results: For the FullFire laser probe, the DeepoLITT model achieved temperature prediction error with average values ranging from 1.16±0.40% to 2.92±0.25%, and peak values ranging from 4.26±1.31% to 14.94±0.43% as data noise increased from 0% to 20%. For the SideFire laser probe, the model achieved temperature prediction error with average values ranging from 3.79±0.53% to 5.13±1.00% and peak values ranging from 15.18±7.15% to 20.75±2.84%. For thermal dose assessment, at the noise-free level for the FullFire laser probe, the model exhibited strong spatial agreement with FEM references, yielding DSCs of 0.96±0.02, 0.97±0.21, and 0.96±0.21 with corresponding HDs of 0.09±0.08 mm, 0.07±0.07 mm, and 0.06±0.08 mm at 2–, 10–, and 60–minute CEM43 thresholds. For the SideFire laser probe, the model achieved DSCs of 0.96±0.02, 0.97±0.21, and 0.96±0.21, with corresponding HDs of 0.20±0.31mm, 0.11±0.30 mm, and 0.15±0.31 mm, respectively. As the noise level increases, these DSC values show a decreasing trend, and the HD values increase. In terms of computational efficiency, the DeepoLITT model inferences temperature maps with 0.04±0.05 seconds per 3D sample ([31 × 31 × 3] grid), compared to 24.32±2.12 seconds required by the FEM solver. Conclusions: The study with synthetic data demonstrates the proposed model is an accurate and rapid method in predicting thermal dose. After testing clinical data, the method has high feasibility to be deployed in real clinical environment.

title: Sc‑HistoMorphomics: A General Framework for High‑throughput, Multimodal Profiling of Nuclear Morphology in Tissues.
abstract: Quantitative cellular morphology provides a rich but underutilized window into cell identity and state. We introduce sc‑HistoMorphomics, a scalable framework for profiling nuclear morphology in whole‑slide H&E images and correlating these measurements with spatial transcriptomics data. Our pipeline combines deep‑learning based segmentation with 194 interpretable morphometric features capturing nuclear shape, eosin and hematoxylin texture, and neighbourhood architecture, enabling high‑throughput, multimodal characterization of tissue organization. Applied to endometrium, breast cancer tissue, and pancreas, sc-HistoMorphomics revealed conserved high‑dimensional feature structure across tissues and reproducible association between morphology and gene expression. Eosin‑based texture features were associated with senescence signatures in endometrium, and morphology-based clustering recapitulated broad stromal, lymphocyte, and epithelial tumor cell classes in breast cancer. In pancreas, negative correlations between CDKN1A and multiple morphological features were consistent across cell types and donors. Together, these results establish sc‑HistoMorphomics as a generalizable and interpretable tool for linking morphology with spatially resolved molecular state across diverse tissues.

title: Fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models and typed decisions for classifying findings in chest CT reports: paired English-Japanese internal testing and external testing on naturally written Japanese reports
abstract: Purpose: To compare fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models (LLMs) and typed decisions (per-finding yes/no questions answered with a probability) for classifying 18 findings in chest CT reports, and to identify when typed decisions help. Methods: This retrospective study used public data. The internal test set comprised 150 CT-RATE reports with paired Japanese translations at three quality levels; the external test set, 243 naturally written Japanese reports with human annotations (RR-Findings). We compared ModernBERT encoders fine-tuned on 20,444 reports, generative LLMs (gpt-6-luna, Qwen3.8-27B, MedGemma), and typed decisions with Jev, the Decisions API and Qwen. Thresholds fixed on 450 development reports were applied unchanged externally. The primary metric was micro-F1; case-level paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for 11 internal comparisons. Results: Encoders were best internally (English 0.9853; radiologist-checked Japanese 0.9576) and exceeded Jev (differences 0.0367, 95% CI 0.0258-0.0484; 0.0336, 0.0215-0.0464). Externally, Jev (0.8844) lay within the encoder seed range (0.8656-0.9144), exceeded the three generative conditions tested externally (best 0.8564) and the Decisions API (0.8177), and had the smallest internal-to-external decrease (-0.0396). An encoder trained on 2,044 reports reached 0.8226 externally. Typed-versus-generated differences changed direction across models and test sets. At a fixed threshold of 0.5, Jev fell to 0.7753 externally. Conclusion: Fine-tuned encoders performed best with ample in-distribution labels. Although threshold-dependent, Jev, with thresholds fitted on only 450 labeled reports, fell within the encoder seed range externally and exceeded the generative LLMs and an encoder trained on 2,044 reports, making it an option when labels are scarce.

title: Circulating miRNA profiling identifies hsa-miR-23a-3p and a three-miRNA signature associated with serous ovarian cancer
abstract: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC) is the most lethal subtype of epithelial ovarian cancer, highlighting the need for minimally invasive biomarkers that support disease detection and molecular characterization. Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as promising candidates, although their clinical applicability remains limited by methodological variability and insufficient validation. Plasma samples from 100 individuals (50 patients with ovarian cancer and 50 cancer-free controls) were initially collected from four biobanks. Following quality control, 94 samples (47 patients and 47 controls) were included in the final analysis. Eight candidate miRNAs were quantified using RT-qPCR, and relative expression was assessed following global mean normalization. Differential expression was evaluated using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, while discriminatory performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Three-miRNA logistic regression models were additionally explored using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation. Among the eight candidates, hsa-miR-23a-3p exhibited significantly lower circulating expression in patients with ovarian cancer than in controls (p = 2.14 x 10^-5), achieving an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.755 (95% CI, 0.657-0.852), with 93.6% sensitivity and 53.2% specificity at the selected threshold. Exploratory analysis across FIGO stages revealed heterogeneous expression patterns, although the limited number of early-stage cases precluded definitive conclusions regarding stage-specific performance. A three-miRNA signature comprising hsa-miR-23a-3p, hsa-miR-21-5p, and hsa-miR-20a-5p achieved an apparent AUC of 0.798. However, repeated cross-validation yielded a mean AUC of 0.716 +/- 0.022, indicating reduced performance after internal validation. Variability in exogenous spike-in Ct values and the marked imbalance in biobank representation between study groups highlighted potential pre-analytical confounding. Circulating hsa-miR-23a-3p showed moderate discriminatory performance between patients with ovarian cancer and cancer-free controls, supporting its further investigation as a candidate liquid biopsy biomarker. Although combining three miRNAs improved apparent classification performance, this advantage was not established through internal validation. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for sample provenance, technical variability, and model overfitting when evaluating circulating miRNA signatures. Independent validation in appropriately balanced cohorts is required before clinical applicability can be established.

title: Pyrenophora teres f. teres uses specialized infection structures to facilitate effector-driven promotion of in planta colonization on barley
abstract: Pyrenophora teres f. teres is a necrotrophic fungal pathogen that causes net form net blotch (NFNB) of barley. Infection of susceptible barley leaves initially causes dot-like lesions that progress to transverse and longitudinal striations, that form the net-like pattern of necrosis for which the disease was named. While the complex genetic architecture of the P. teres f. teres-barley interaction involves both dominant resistance and susceptibility and quantitative resistance, the in planta infection structures, compatible infection timeline, and the influence of effectors remain poorly defined. This study used fluorescent staining and confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) to define infection structures and characterize the compatible infection timeline of P. teres f. teres. Using CLSM in conjunction with image-segmentation machine learning, we generated a clear comparative infection timeline showing how P. teres f. teres isolates harboring zero, one, or two virulence effector alleles infect the barley cultivar Rika. We believe that the effector genes VR1 and VR2 contributed to virulence in a synergistic manner. The effector genes combined presence accelerated the timing and spread of programmed cell death, resulting in significantly greater hyphal volume and visibly more severe macroscopic lesion development. This suggests that P. teres f. teres uses specialized infection structures alongside effectors to maximize fungal colonization and hyphal positioning to optimize nutrient uptake, perpetuating its polycyclic life cycle.

title: Automated aortoiliac calcification segmentation from arterial-phase computed tomography scans: development and validation
abstract: Introduction: Arterial calcium is widely used as a biomarker for coronary artery disease but is underutilized in peripheral artery disease (PAD) due to challenges in automated measurement. We developed a fully automated deep-learning pipeline for aortoiliac calcium measurement from arterial-phase, contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT angiography (CTA). Methods: Two nnU-Net models perform aortoiliac arterial segmentation and identification of calcified voxels. We trained on 56 CT scans and validated on 106 scans by comparing the pipeline's calcium estimation from CTA against calcium burden on corresponding non-contrast phase CT within manually segmented arterial contours across radiodensity thresholds of 100-1,000 HU. Using the threshold maximizing correlation, we performed linear regression with five-fold cross-validation between pipeline-estimated and non-contrast calcium quantities, and risk reclassification analysis to compare pipeline-predicted and non-contrast-derived calcium burden quartiles using quadratically weighted kappa. Results: Non-contrast calcium voxels [≥]400 HU correlated best with CTA calcium burden (aortic Pearson r=0.952; iliofemoral Pearson r=0.955). Five-fold cross-validation of non-contrast calcium volume prediction ([≥]400 HU) from pipeline-estimated calcium burden demonstrated aggregated Pearson r>0.91 for all held-out folds in all regions. In risk reclassification analysis, quadratically weighted kappa for agreement of predicted and ground truth calcium quartile classification was k=0.88 for aorta, k=0.84 for bilateral iliofemoral arteries, and k=0.80 for combined. Conclusion: Aortoiliac calcium burden can be automatically quantified from CTA with excellent reproducibility against calcium voxels [≥]400 HU on non-contrast imaging. Quantification of this important biomarker expands opportunities for improved peripheral vascular disease diagnosis and risk prediction.

title: NeuroImgAgent: a multi-agent platform for cross-species fMRI analysis with evidence-gated quality control
abstract: Cross-species functional MRI analysis requires coordinating specialized workflows and assessing intermediate outputs. We present NeuroImgAgent, a multi-agent platform driven by large language models that translates natural-language requests into workflows for humans, macaques, rats and mice. Quantitative checks and vision-language model assessments determine whether processing continues, enters bounded recovery or stops. Across 268 paired cases, preprocessing metrics were broadly comparable to those of fMRIPrep, AFNI and RABIES. With GPT-5.5, NeuroImgAgent corrected 111 of 120 induced orientation errors and passed all 52 intent-recognition and planning tasks, 8 of 9 recovery tasks and 11 of 14 tool-construction tasks on NeuroAgentBench. In 120 paired challenge cases, the full configuration increased usability from 76.7% to 92.5%, as assessed by blinded experts, and reduced unusable outputs delivered without warning from 18.3% to 4.2% of cases relative to quality-control ablation.

title: Retinal Vessel Volume Density and Intraoperative Cortical Vascular Phenotypes in Moyamoya Disease
abstract: Background: Angiographic staging describes large-artery stenosis and collateral evolution in moyamoya disease but does not directly depict the cortical surface vasculature, which can vary among patients with similar Suzuki stages. We examined whether a side-matched three-dimensional retinal vascular measure was associated with intraoperative cortical vascular phenotypes after accounting for Suzuki stage. Methods This prospective single-center cohort included 52 patients with moyamoya disease who underwent combined direct and indirect revascularization; 48 had analyzable retinal vessel volume density (RVVD) in the side-matched eye. RVVD was defined as the percentage of the corresponding retinal tissue volume occupied by three-dimensional optical coherence tomography angiography vascular signal within the central 6 x 6-mm region from the retinal nerve fiber layer to the inner plexiform layer. After dural opening and before vascular manipulation, overall cortical vascular richness and arterial, venous, and small-vessel richness were graded from 0 to 3. Associations were evaluated with Spearman correlation and proportional-odds ordinal logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, and ipsilateral Suzuki stage. Results Mean RVVD was 12.92% (SD, 3.30 percentage points). Higher RVVD was associated with greater overall cortical vascular richness (ρ =0.523; bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap 95% CI, 0.279-0.714; P<0.001) and arterial richness (ρ =0.522; 95% CI, 0.261-0.714; P<0.001). Per 1-SD higher RVVD, the adjusted cumulative odds ratio for being in a higher richness category was 3.92 (95% CI, 1.82-8.44; P<0.001) for overall cortical vascular richness and 4.31 (95% CI, 1.92-9.70; P<0.001) for arterial richness. Conclusions In moyamoya disease, higher side-matched RVVD was associated with richer overall and arterial cortical vascular phenotypes at revascularization surgery, independent of Suzuki stage. Three-dimensional retinal vascular imaging may therefore provide a noninvasive, side-specific preoperative measure of cortical vascular remodeling.

title: [MRI of suspected bone and soft tissue sarcomas - an overview].
abstract: Sarcomas are rare malignant tumors of connective and supportive tissues, associated with relatively poor five-year survival. According to Swedish patient care bundles ("standardiserat vårdförlopp"), MRI should be performed at local radiology departments before a possible referral to a sarcoma center when there is a strong suspicion of a soft tissue sarcoma, highlighting the need for adequate knowledge of appopriate MRI protocols. For soft tissue lesions, MRI is diagnostic only for a few entities, such as simple lipomas. Most muskuloskeletal tumors, however, require biopsy for definitive diagnosis. Consequently, MRI is primarily used to assess tumor extent prior to biopsy and potential surgery. The Swedish Society of Musculoskeletal Radiology (SFMSR) recommends that an MRI protocol for musculoskeletal tumors should always consist of at least the following three sequences: coronal STIR FSE, axial T1-weighted FSE, and axial T2-weighted FSE. Coronal STIR is mainly used for tumor detection and evaluation of lipomatous lesions. Axial T1 is primarily used to assess intraosseous tumor extent and characterize lipomatous lesions. Axial T2 is primarily used to evaluate soft tissue tumor extension and extraosseous components of bone tumors.

title: Presacral Myelolipoma Mimicking Liposarcoma Complicated by Massive Intraoperative Hemorrhage: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Myelolipoma is a benign tumor composed of mature adipose tissue and hematopoietic elements. Extra-adrenal lesions can occur in the presacral region and may mimic liposarcoma. Resection of a large presacral tumor can also cause life-threatening hemorrhage. We report a presacral myelolipoma that was difficult to diagnose preoperatively and was complicated by massive intraoperative hemorrhage. Case presentation A 71-year-old woman had an incidentally detected 75 × 75 × 125-mm presacral mass with mixed fatty and solid components on contrast-enhanced CT. MRI showed restricted diffusion, and fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT showed mild uptake (maximum standardized uptake value, 3.93). No growth occurred over approximately 3 months. Because liposarcoma could not be excluded, the patient chose open resection without biopsy for diagnosis and treatment. During cranial dissection along the anterior sacrum, massive bleeding occurred from the right internal iliac venous system, and systolic blood pressure decreased to 50-60 mmHg. Manual compression was insufficient, and massive transfusion was initiated. Intraoperatively, a vein communicating with the right internal iliac vein was found to enter the tumor, and the main trunk of the right internal iliac vein was ligated near its junction with the right common iliac vein. Persistent bleeding required ligation of a tumor-entering branch of the right internal iliac artery; the arterial main trunk was preserved. Hemostasis was prioritized, and the tumor was removed in 2 pieces; the capsule was disrupted without macroscopic tumor spillage. Diffuse presacral venous plexus bleeding was controlled with electrocautery and oxidized cellulose. Operative time was 3 h 21 min, and blood loss was 4850 mL; 10 units of leukocyte-reduced red blood cells and 6 units of fresh frozen plasma were transfused. Histopathological examination established the diagnosis of myelolipoma. No vascular complications occurred, and contrast-enhanced CT at approximately 1 year showed no residual or recurrent tumor. Conclusions Presacral myelolipoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of fat-containing presacral tumors. In large tumors, the relationship with the internal iliac vessels and presacral venous plexus should be carefully assessed, and adequate blood products, early vascular control, and source-specific hemostatic techniques should be prepared before resection.

title: Emergency Resection for Perforated Small Bowel Metastasis from Primary Lung Cancer During Systemic Therapy: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Small bowel metastases from lung cancer may remain clinically occult until serious complications, including obstruction, bleeding, and perforation, occur. We report a case of perforated jejunal metastasis with a synchronous ileal metastasis at high risk of obstruction, identified during emergency surgery while several previously documented extraintestinal lesions had decreased in size. Case presentation A 75-year-old woman with metastatic non-small cell lung carcinoma favoring adenocarcinoma had a programmed death-ligand 1 tumor proportion score of 95% and no targetable alteration on the companion-diagnostic panel. Pembrolizumab monotherapy (200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks) was administered for 4 cycles; no antiangiogenic agent had been administered concurrently or previously. Eleven days after the 4th dose, she developed acute abdominal pain. CT showed focal small bowel wall thickening, adjacent extraluminal air, diffuse bowel edema, and ascites. Emergency surgery revealed a perforated jejunal tumor approximately 20 cm distal to the ligament of Treitz. Systematic examination of the entire small bowel identified a 2nd, nearly circumferential ileal tumor approximately 15 cm proximal to the terminal ileum with marked luminal narrowing; both lesions were resected. Histopathological examination showed metastatic poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of pulmonary origin. Neither tumor necrosis nor a histological treatment effect was identified, and the non-neoplastic mucosa showed no findings suggestive of immune checkpoint inhibitor-related enteritis. The patient was discharged on POD 19. Pembrolizumab was not resumed. PET-CT on POD 30 demonstrated widespread disease progression, and the patient transitioned to best supportive care. She died on POD 61 without recurrent gastrointestinal perforation, obstruction, or bleeding. Conclusions Clinically occult small bowel metastases may present with perforation or impending obstruction during systemic therapy even while previously documented lesions at other sites decrease in size. Because the intestinal lesions were not identifiable before treatment, true discordant progression could not be established. Histopathological findings supported direct tumor-related perforation rather than treatment-induced tumor necrosis or immune-mediated enteritis. Emergency source control and systematic examination of the entire small bowel may identify additional lesions that alter operative management.

title: Posterior Mediastinal Schwannoma Extending into the Retroperitoneum Resected through a Thoracoabdominal Approach.
abstract: Introduction Posterior mediastinal schwannomas are generally resected through a thoracic approach. However, giant tumors extending beyond the diaphragm into the retroperitoneum present unique technical challenges because of their proximity to major vascular structures and the potential risk of neurological complications. We report a case of a giant posterior mediastinal schwannoma successfully resected through a thoracoabdominal approach. Case presentation A woman in her 70s was found to have a 10-cm posterior mediastinal mass during a routine health examination. She initially chose observation, but the tumor gradually enlarged to 13 cm over 6 years. Fluorodeoxyglucose-PET demonstrated increased uptake (maximum standardized uptake value, 9.2 at 60 min and 10.4 at 120 min). CT showed extension from the T9 to the L2 level, with displacement of the right kidney and compression of the inferior vena cava (IVC). Because malignancy could not be completely excluded and further growth was considered likely to increase the technical difficulty of resection, surgery was performed. A right thoracotomy was initially performed, but adequate exposure of the caudal tumor was not obtained. The incision was therefore extended to the abdomen, followed by midline laparotomy and diaphragmatic incision. The liver and right kidney were mobilized, and the IVC and right renal artery were secured before deep dissection. Feeding arteries from the right T10-T12 segmental/lumbar branches were divided close to the tumor capsule, and the tumor was completely removed en bloc. The operative time was 4 h 33 min, with 691 mL blood loss. Intraoperative milk administration confirmed the absence of chyle leakage. The postoperative course was uneventful, without neurological deficit or chylothorax, and the patient was discharged on POD 10. Histopathological examination confirmed a benign schwannoma, and the patient remained recurrence-free at the 9-month follow-up. Conclusions A thoracoabdominal approach provides excellent surgical exposure for giant posterior mediastinal tumors extending beyond the diaphragm. Careful management of segmental arteries and meticulous attention to thoracic duct injury may contribute to safe resection while minimizing neurological and lymphatic complications.

title: Young-Onset Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma Developing after Allogeneic Bone Marrow Transplantation for Fanconi Anemia: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Fanconi anemia (FA), a rare genetic disorder, is characterized by defective DNA repair and an increased risk of early-onset squamous cell carcinoma. Although hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) improves survival, long-term survivors experience a high risk of secondary malignancies, including esophageal cancer. Owing to extreme sensitivity to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, treatment of FA-associated esophageal cancer is particularly challenging. Case presentation A 22-year-old woman with FA who had undergone unrelated allogeneic bone marrow transplantation in childhood developed esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Preoperative endoscopy, CT, and PET showed no lymph node or distant metastases, and the tumor was staged as cT2N0M0, cStage II. Because of the anticipated severe toxicity of DNA-damaging chemotherapy and radiotherapy in FA, an upfront surgery strategy was selected. Thoracoscopic subtotal esophagectomy with 2-field lymph-node dissection achieved R0 resection. Despite the absence of radiologically or macroscopically suspicious lymph nodes, histopathological examination revealed adventitial invasion, marked lymphovascular invasion, and metastases in 3 of 25 lymph nodes (pT3N2M0, pStage IIIB). Postoperative systemic therapy was considered, but its initiation was deferred because of incomplete postoperative recovery and concern regarding treatment toxicity. Multiple recurrences became evident 4 months after surgery, before systemic therapy could be reconsidered, and the patient died 10 months postoperatively. Conclusions This case highlights the therapeutic dilemma in FA-associated esophageal cancer between substantial toxicity from standard cytotoxic therapy and the risk of undertreatment with upfront surgery. The marked discrepancy between clinical and pathological staging illustrates the difficulty of excluding occult nodal or systemic disease when neoadjuvant therapy cannot readily be administered. Previous reports suggest that reduced-dose chemotherapy or chemoradiotherapy may retain antitumor activity but can still cause substantial toxicity, indicating an extremely narrow therapeutic window. Treatment therefore requires individualized multidisciplinary decision-making, while further accumulation of detailed data on treatment intensity, toxicity, response, and outcomes is needed.

title: [Recent advances in brain injury in preterm infants].
abstract: The incidence of brain injury in preterm infants is high, and periventricular-intraventricular hemorrhage and white matter injury are the most common types. The occurrence of these two types of brain injuries results from prenatal, intrapartum, and postnatal factors, and the pathogenesis is complex, involving hypoxia-ischemia, immune and inflammatory responses, and immaturity of brain development. In recent years, advanced technologies such as functional near-infrared spectroscopy, amplitude-integrated electroencephalography, cranial ultrasonography, and multimodal magnetic resonance imaging have been widely applied for early detection of brain injury in preterm infants and for the assessment of severity and prognosis, although the clinical value of different modalities varies. Preterm infants with severe brain injury have a poor prognosis, and current preventive and therapeutic options remain limited in clinical practice. Of these, glucocorticoid therapy is the most well-established, whereas erythropoietin and stem cell therapies remain exploratory. Therefore, avoidance of high-risk factors, early prediction, effective prevention and treatment, and improvement of prognosis remain pressing issues in clinical practice and research.

title: [Research progress on correlation between non-contact anterior cruciate ligament injury and bone bruise].
abstract: Objective To review the research progress on the correlation between non-contact anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury and bone bruise. Methods Relevant literature on non-contact ACL injury and bone bruise published in recent years was reviewed. The imaging characteristics and injury mechanisms of bone bruise, factors affecting bone bruise distribution, the associations between bone bruise and combined intra-articular injuries, and the impact of bone bruise on postoperative outcomes after ACL reconstruction were summarized and analyzed. Results Bone bruise is a common MRI finding in non-contact ACL injury, mainly involving the lateral femoral condyle and lateral tibial plateau. The typical "kissing" bone bruise pattern can reflect the abnormal loading condition of the knee joint at the moment of injury and provides important imaging evidence for inferring the injury mechanism of ACL rupture. The occurrence and distribution of bone bruise may be influenced by factors such as age, osseous morphology of the knee, and meniscal anatomical characteristics. The extent, location, and severity of bone bruise are associated with knee laxity, anterolateral ligament injury, meniscal tears, and articular cartilage injury to varying degrees. Among these, the association between lateral compartment bone bruise and lateral meniscal injury is relatively well established, while bone bruise of the medial tibial plateau may indicate occult posterior horn injury of the medial meniscus. Bone bruise may also be associated with early postoperative pain and recovery of knee range of motion after ACL reconstruction, and may increase the risk of cartilage degeneration and post-traumatic osteoarthritis. However, its predictive value for mid- and long-term knee function and clinical outcomes remains inconclusive. Conclusion Bone bruise can reflect, to some extent, the loading mechanism and severity of non-contact ACL injury, and provides important clues for identifying associated structural injuries and evaluating prognosis. However, the grading and assessment criteria for bone bruise remain unstandardized, and controversies remain regarding its associations with certain combined injuries and long-term clinical outcomes. Further standardized, large-scale, multi-center, and long-term follow-up studies are required to clarify the clinical value of bone bruise in the assessment and prognostic evaluation of ACL injury.

title: [Effect of endoscopy-assisted anterior cervical discectomy and fusion on single-level cervical spondylotic radiculopathy].
abstract: Objective To compare the clinical efficacy and safety of endoscopy-assisted anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (Endo-ACDF) versus conventional ACDF in the treatment of single-level cervical spondylotic radiculopathy (CSR). Methods Ninety-nine patients with single-level CSR treated between January 2023 and January 2025 were retrospectively enrolled, including 46 patients who underwent Endo-ACDF (Endo-ACDF group) and 53 patients who underwent conventional ACDF (ACDF group). Propensity score matching was performed, and 62 patients (31 in each group) were finally enrolled. Baseline characteristics, including age, gender, body mass index, disease duration, affected segment, and preoperative visual analogue scale (VAS) score, Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score, neck disability index (NDI), C 2-7 Cobb angle and height of the affected intervertebral space, were comparable between the two groups after matching ( P >0.05). The outcome indicators were compared between groups, including perioperative parameters (operation time, incision length, intraoperative blood loss, and hospital stay); VAS score, JOA score, and NDI before operation and at 3 days, 3 months, 6 months and 12 months after operation; radiographic parameters (C 2-7 Cobb angle, height of the affected intervertebral space, and interbody fusion); occurrence of complications. Results All operations were completed successfully. Compared with the ACDF group, the Endo-ACDF group had a shorter incision length, less intraoperative blood loss, and a shorter hospital stay, but a longer operation time, all showing significant differences ( P <0.05). All patients were followed up 12 months. In both groups, VAS score, JOA score, and NDI at each postoperative time point significantly improved compared with the preoperative values ( P <0.05). The Endo-ACDF group showed better VAS scores at 3 days, 3 months, and 6 months and better NDI scores at 3 days and 3 months than the ACDF group ( P <0.05). At 12 months after operation, the C 2-7 Cobb angle and the height of the affected intervertebral space significantly improved compared with the preoperative values in the two groups ( P <0.05), while the changes from baseline in these two parameters did not differ significantly between the two groups ( P >0.05). Bone fusion was achieved in all patients of both groups, with a fusion rate of 100%. The incidences of complications were 3.23% (1/31) in the Endo-ACDF group and 9.68% (3/31) in the ACDF group, with no significant difference ( P> 0.05). Conclusion Endo-ACDF achieved comparable efficacy to conventional ACDF in the treatment of single-level CSR, with the advantages of a clearer operative field, less surgical trauma, and faster early postoperative symptom relief and functional recovery.

title: [Early effectiveness of patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum blocks for hip revision in patients with Paprosky type Ⅲ massive acetabular bone defects].
abstract: Objective To evaluate the early clinical and radiographic outcomes of patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum blocks for the reconstruction of Paprosky type Ⅲ massive acetabular bone defects in hip revision. Methods The clinical data of 17 patients (17 hips) with Paprosky type Ⅲ massive acetabular bone defects undergoing revision after hip arthroplasty between January 2022 and January 2025 were retrospectively analyzed. The cohort comprised 6 males and 11 females, with a mean age of 59.4 years (range, 37-80 years). Nine patients had Paprosky type ⅢA defects and 8 had type ⅢB defects, including 5 with pelvic discontinuity. All patients underwent acetabular side (9 cases) or both acetabular and femoral components (8 cases) reconstruction with patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum blocks combined with revision acetabular cups. Harris hip score (HHS) and visual analogue scale (VAS) score were compared between preoperative and last follow-up. The position of radiographic hip center of rotation (rCOR), acetabular cup inclination and anteversion, osseointegration, and implant stability were evaluated by anteroposterior pelvic X-ray films and CT, and perioperative complications and re-revision were recorded. Results The operation was successfully completed in all patients, with a mean operation time of 141.2 minutes (range, 80-280 minutes) and a mean intraoperative blood loss of 752.9 mL (range, 300-1 500 mL). All patients completed follow-up, with a mean duration of 22.1 months (range, 13-41 months). At last follow-up, the HHS score significantly increased from 37.0±5.8 to 87.9±3.0, while the VAS score significantly decreased from 6.0 (5.5, 7.0) to 0.0 (0.0, 1.0) ( P <0.05). The horizontal rCOR distance on the operated side improved significantly when compared with the preoperative value ( P <0.05) and did not differ significantly from that on the contralateral side ( P >0.05). The vertical rCOR distance decreased significantly ( P <0.05) but remained greater than that on the contralateral side ( P <0.05). At last follow-up, all acetabular reconstructions remained radiographically stable, with an acetabular cup inclination of (41.87±4.38)° and an acetabular cup anteversion of (19.47±3.77)°. No intraoperative screw penetration through the inner pelvic cortex or neurovascular injury was recorded. No heterotopic ossification, clinically significant limb-length discrepancy, implant mismatch requiring additional adjustment or component replacement, tantalum blocks migration, screw loosening or breakage, or aseptic loosening was observed. Postoperative venous thrombosis occurred in 2 patients, both of whom improved following treatment. No other major complication was reported. Conclusion Patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum blocks demonstrated favorable early clinical and radiographic outcomes in the reconstruction of Paprosky type Ⅲ massive acetabular bone defects, with improvements in hip function, pain relief, radiographic stability, and restoration of the hip center of rotation. Larger multicenter and random clinical trials with longer follow-up are warranted to establish long-term outcomes and potential advantages over alternative reconstruction techniques.

title: [Clinical application of patient-specific three-dimensional-printed porous tantalum biological proximal interphalangeal joint prostheses].
abstract: Objective To investigate the effectiveness and safety of patient-specific three-dimensional (3D)-printed porous tantalum biological proximal interphalangeal joint (PIP) prostheses for the treatment of PIP osteoarthritis. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 17 patients with PIP osteoarthritis who underwent arthroplasty using patient-specific 3D-printed porous tantalum biological PIP prostheses between January 2023 and January 2025. The study population comprised 11 men and 6 women, with a mean age of 38 years (range, 22-67 years). The affected fingers included the middle finger in 9 patients, index finger in 4, ring finger in 2, and little finger in 2. Preoperatively, the active PIP flexion range of motion (ROM) was (29.73±11.58)°, and the extension ROM was (14.62±7.10)°. The preoperative visual analogue scale (VAS) score for pain was 5.6±1.1, and the Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) score was 37.0±4.5. The operation time, intraoperative blood loss, and perioperative complications were recorded. Active PIP flexion and extension ROM, VAS scores, and DASH score were compared between preoperation and last follow-up. X-ray film evaluations were performed to assess coronal plane alignment, periprosthetic radiolucent lines, and evidence of prosthetic deformation or fracture. Results All 17 procedures were successfully completed. The mean operation time was 67 minutes (range, 57-81 minutes), and the mean intraoperative blood loss was 50 mL (range, 30-65 mL). No perioperative complication, including skin necrosis or infection, was observed. All patients completed follow-up, with a mean follow-up duration of 8 months (range, 6-21 months). At last follow-up, the active PIP flexion ROM increased to (84.35±7.97)°, the VAS score decreased to 0.8±0.9, and the DASH score improved to 11.0±5.5, all showing significant didifferences when compared with preoperative values ( P< 0.05); the extension ROM was (21.48±12.26)°, showing no significant didifference ( P >0.05). Radiographic assessment at last follow-up demonstrated satisfactory coronal plane alignment in all patients. No periprosthetic radiolucent lines, prosthetic deformation, fracture, or subsidence was identified. Conclusion Patient-specific 3D-printed porous tantalum biological PIP arthroplasty appears to be a promising surgical option for the treatment of PIP osteoarthritis. This technique may effectively relieve pain, improve joint flexion ROM and hand function, and provide satisfactory short-term radiographic stability.

title: Decreased Synovial Fluid SLC7A11 and GPX4 Levels Correlate with Knee Osteoarthritis Disease Severity.
abstract: Background Ferroptosis has been suggested to play a role in the pathogenesis of primary knee osteoarthritis (OA). The current study aimed to explore the potential relationship between the concentrations of SLC7A11 and GPX4 in serum and synovial fluid (SF) and the severity of knee OA. Methods A total of 120 patients with knee OA and 120 healthy controls were included in this study. Serum and SF levels of SLC7A11 and GPX4 were measured using ELISA before and after a comprehensive therapeutic intervention. Radiographic severity of OA was evaluated using the Kellgren-Lawrence (K-L) grading system. Clinical severity was assessed via Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoar-thritis Index (WOMAC) scores. Levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6) and matrix metalloproteinase-3 (MMP-3) were also analyzed. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was employed to evaluate the diagnostic utility of SLC7A11 and GPX4 levels in relation to K-L grades. Results Serum levels of SLC7A11 and GPX4 did not show significant differences between knee OA patients and healthy controls. However, patients with K-L grade 4 exhibited statistically significant lower concentrations of SLC7A11 and GPX4 in SF compared to those with K-L grades 2 and 3. Furthermore, SF levels of these proteins were significantly lower in patients with K-L grade 3 compared to those with grade 2. Negative correlations were observed between SF levels of SLC7A11 and GPX4 and K-L grades, as well as with SF levels of IL-6 and MMP-3. SF concentrations of SLC7A11 and GPX4 were also inversely correlated with VAS and WOMAC scores. ROC analysis indicated that both SLC7A11 and GPX4 demonstrated good diagnostic value for assessing radiographic progression in knee OA. Conclusions These results indicate that SLC7A11 and GPX4 may function as potential biomarkers for monitoring disease progression and therapeutic efficacy in knee osteoarthritis.

title: Artificial Intelligence Versus Human Interpretation in Diagnostic Radiology: A Systematic Review of Diagnostic Accuracy and Operational Efficiency.
abstract: Rising imaging workload and a shortage of radiology specialists have driven interest in artificial intelligence (AI) to improve diagnostic speed and accuracy. This systematic review, without meta-analysis, describes how AI affects diagnostic accuracy and operational efficiency compared with human interpretation in diagnostic radiology. Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) and Cochrane guidance, PubMed, ClinicalKey, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar were searched on 11 April 2026 for studies published from January 2019 onwards. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and a Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2)-based risk-of-bias assessment. Twenty-one studies were included: 11 compared standalone AI with human readers, six compared AI-assisted with unassisted readers, and four reported both; 18 evaluated task-specific image-analysis AI and three evaluated generative AI models. Because no subgroup was homogeneous enough to pool, we synthesised results narratively and stratified them by comparison type, AI category, imaging modality, and study quality. Standalone image-analysis AI achieved high sensitivity for fractures and selected chest findings but performed less well on subtle findings and lower-quality images, and in one computed tomography-referenced comparison a radiologist outperformed AI. AI assistance improved reader performance more consistently, particularly among less experienced readers. Generative models did not reach specialist performance on complex tasks. Efficiency gains were concentrated in normal studies, and the only randomised trial found lower mammography screen-reading workload with similar early screening performance. No study assessed patient outcomes, and 18 of 21 studies were retrospective. This evidence supports AI only as a supervised, complementary tool; improvements in diagnostic accuracy should not be equated with clinical benefit.

title: From Spiradenocarcinoma to Spiradenoma: A Case of Histopathological Diagnostic Reclassification.
abstract: Spiradenocarcinoma is a rare malignant cutaneous adnexal neoplasm that may arise from a preexisting spiradenoma. Distinguishing benign from malignant lesions can be challenging, and diagnostic classification has important implications for treatment and follow-up. A 37-year-old woman presented with an approximately 3-cm erythematous-violaceous nodule on the right ankle that had been present for five years and had recently grown rapidly. The initial histopathological assessment described a malignant epithelial neoplasm compatible with spiradenocarcinoma associated with a benign spiradenoma component. The patient underwent wider surgical re-excision with clinical margins exceeding 1 cm, and computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no metastatic disease. No residual neoplasm was identified in the re-excision specimen. Subsequent review of the original histological slides at a second laboratory identified a well-circumscribed, lobulated, solid-cystic dermal lesion with two distinct epithelial cell populations and an interspersed lymphocytic infiltrate, without infiltrative growth, nuclear atypia, mitotic activity, or necrosis in the reviewed material. The diagnosis was revised to benign spiradenoma. Immunohistochemistry supported the diagnosis of an eccrine neoplasm. This case illustrates the diagnostic challenges in distinguishing spiradenoma from spiradenocarcinoma and the clinical implications of discrepant histopathological assessments. Morphological evaluation remains central to classification, while immunohistochemistry provides complementary information.

title: Beyond Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: A Narrative Review of the Radiological and Endoscopic Features of Solid Pancreatic Neoplasms.
abstract: Solid pancreatic neoplasms comprise a heterogeneous group of tumors with distinct histopathological characteristics, biological behaviors, and therapeutic implications. Although pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the predominant malignancy, non-ductal neoplasms, including pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma (PACC), pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs), solid pseudopapillary neoplasms (SPNs), and pancreatoblastoma, represent important diagnostic alternatives. This narrative review aims to summarize and compare the radiological and endoscopic features of solid pancreatic neoplasms, emphasizing their differential diagnosis and the contribution of endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided tissue acquisition to diagnostic characterization. A narrative review of the literature was conducted, focusing on studies addressing CT, MRI, conventional and contrast-enhanced EUS, elastography, and EUS-guided tissue acquisition in the characterization and differential diagnosis of solid pancreatic tumors. PDAC typically demonstrates infiltrative growth and reduced enhancement, whereas non-ductal neoplasms may exhibit well-defined margins and variable vascular patterns. PACC may present as a well-circumscribed mass with heterogeneous enhancement and areas of cystic degeneration, while PanNETs frequently demonstrate hypervascularity, and SPNs often exhibit mixed solid and cystic components. However, substantial imaging overlap limits reliable histological differentiation. Beyond the morphological and vascular characterization provided by EUS, EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy (EUS-FNB), combined with histological and immunohistochemical analysis, plays a crucial role in establishing a definitive diagnosis, particularly for uncommon neoplasms. Emerging technologies, including radiomics and artificial intelligence (AI), offer promising opportunities for improving diagnostic characterization. Accurate differentiation of solid pancreatic neoplasms requires an integrated approach combining cross-sectional imaging, EUS, and histopathological assessment. Recognizing characteristic imaging patterns and understanding their limitations may improve diagnostic accuracy and guide appropriate tissue acquisition and therapeutic decision-making.

Although pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the predominant malignancy, non-ductal neoplasms, including pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma (PACC), pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs), solid pseudopapillary neoplasms (SPNs), and pancreatoblastoma, represent important diagnostic alternatives. This narrative review aims to summarize and compare the radiological and endoscopic features of solid pancreatic neoplasms, emphasizing their differential diagnosis and the contribution of endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided tissue acquisition to diagnostic characterization. A narrative review of the literature was conducted, focusing on studies addressing CT, MRI, conventional and contrast-enhanced EUS, elastography, and EUS-guided tissue acquisition in the characterization and differential diagnosis of solid pancreatic tumors. PDAC typically demonstrates infiltrative growth and reduced enhancement, whereas non-ductal neoplasms may exhibit well-defined margins and variable vascular patterns. PACC may present as a well-circumscribed mass with heterogeneous enhancement and areas of cystic degeneration, while PanNETs frequently demonstrate hypervascularity, and SPNs often exhibit mixed solid and cystic components. However, substantial imaging overlap limits reliable histological differentiation. Beyond the morphological and vascular characterization provided by EUS, EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy (EUS-FNB), combined with histological and immunohistochemical analysis, plays a crucial role in establishing a definitive diagnosis, particularly for uncommon neoplasms. Emerging technologies, including radiomics and artificial intelligence (AI), offer promising opportunities for improving diagnostic characterization. Accurate differentiation of solid pancreatic neoplasms requires an integrated approach combining cross-sectional imaging, EUS, and histopathological assessment. Recognizing characteristic imaging patterns and understanding their limitations may improve diagnostic accuracy and guide appropriate tissue acquisition and therapeutic decision-making.
